Lifestyle Migration · Methods and supplementary analyses

Moving for a New Lifestyle: Time Use and Migration in the United States
Shizhen Wang · Riordan Frost
Riordan Frost: riordan_frost@harvard.edu

DATA AND RESEARCH DESIGN

Measure places. Link moves. Compare destinations with origins.

01

ATUS: how places live

Aggregate diary minutes into six activity dimensions, then estimate adjusted metropolitan profiles in rolling ten-year windows.

02

ACS: who moves where

Identify actual domestic cross-metropolitan moves. Match current and previous residence separately to metropolitan areas.

03

OD: the lifestyle contrast

For each move, subtract the origin’s score from the destination’s score. Model how this contrast differs by age, education, income and other characteristics.

1. Construct six metropolitan lifestyle measures.

We measure place-based lifestyles using the American Time Use Survey (ATUS), conducted by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. ATUS records how respondents spent the previous day, while its linked Current Population Survey (CPS) file provides demographic characteristics and geographic identifiers. The respondent file also records the diary day of the week, which we control for when estimating metropolitan lifestyle profiles. Our analysis begins with the combined 2003–2025 ATUS activity, respondent and ATUS–CPS files. Guided by the ATUS activity coding lexicon, we sum each respondent’s diary minutes in six categories: personal care, work and education, household activities, social activity, leisure and travel. Table A1 lists the activity codes and activities assigned to each category.

Study-defined groupings from the ATUS activity coding lexicon; ambiguous residual minutes are not forced into the six classes.

For each activity, area profiles adjust for age, sex, race, marital status, education, survey year and diary day of the week. The original area regressions are unweighted; ACS person weights enter the later migration regressions. Scores are standardized separately by activity and rolling window.

2. Match origins and destinations carefully.

To observe moves between places, we use person-level records from the American Community Survey Public Use Microdata Sample (ACS PUMS) for 2015–2019 and 2021–2024. We omit 2020 because the Census Bureau did not release its standard 2020 ACS one-year PUMS following pandemic-related disruptions to data collection. We retain respondents identified as having moved to within the United States during the previous year. The ACS reports their current state and Public Use Microdata Area (PUMA), which identify the destination (D), and their state and migration PUMA (MIGPUMA) of residence one year earlier, which identify the origin (O). A migration PUMA is not necessarily the same geographic unit as a current-residence PUMA; the two sides of a move must therefore be matched using different geographic crosswalks. The ACS also provides respondents’ age, sex, marital status, education, income and other characteristics used in the subsequent analysis.

Following the geographic correspondence developed by IPUMS USA (2023), we assign movers’ origins and destinations to MSAs defined by the 2023 metropolitan delineations. Because the ACS identifies origins using migration PUMAs (MIGPUMAs) but destinations using current-residence PUMAs, we use separate crosswalks for the two ends of each move. We use the crosswalks for 2010-based geographies with ACS observations through 2021 and those for 2020-based geographies from 2022 onward. IPUMS assigns a PUMA or MIGPUMA to an MSA when a majority of its population lies within that MSA and publishes MSA-level omission and commission errors for the resulting correspondence. Its standard metropolitan identification excludes MSAs for which the sum of these errors is 15% or greater. Because geographic ambiguity at either end of a move could distort our comparison, our main analysis applies a more conservative rule at both origin and destination: at least 95% of the relevant PUMA or MIGPUMA population must lie within its assigned MSA, and the IPUMS-published sum of omission and commission errors for that MSA must be below five percentage points. We retain only moves between two different MSAs satisfying this rule. This conservative matching strategy improves the geographic alignment between ACS movers and ATUS metropolitan lifestyle profiles by retaining areas with low published boundary-matching errors.

3. Measure the profiles before the recorded move.

Finally, we restrict the ACS sample to cross-MSA movers, whose origin and destination are in two different metropolitan areas; moves within the same MSA are excluded. We link each move observed in year t to the metropolitan lifestyle profiles ending in year t − 1 at both ends of the move. Using profiles measured before the ACS survey year reduces the possibility that contemporaneous moves contribute to the destination lifestyle measure against which those same moves are compared. For example, an ACS observation from 2015 is matched to profiles estimated using ATUS data from 2005–2014: one for the origin (L1) and one for the destination (L2). We retain observations only when all six lifestyle measures are available for both metropolitan areas. Under the strict geographic rule, 402,385 cross-MSA mover records are identified before the lifestyle link, and 220,817 have complete origin and destination lifestyle profiles. The subsequent regression sample contains 189,114 adults with complete model variables.

4. Estimate six demographic models.

We examine how movers' demographic characteristics are associated with differences between the lifestyle profiles of their destination and origin metropolitan areas. Let i denote an individual mover observed in ACS year t, and let k denote one of the six lifestyle categories. We estimate a separate model for each category:

Sdestination,k,t−1 − Sorigin,k,t−1
= Xi,tβk + μorigin,k + τt,k + εi,t,k

Here, the score indexed by D(i) is the standardized score for lifestyle k in mover i's destination MSA, and the score indexed by O(i) is the corresponding score in the origin MSA. Both scores are estimated from ATUS data in the ten-year window ending in year t−1. Their difference, ΔS, is the destination-minus-origin lifestyle difference associated with mover i; a positive value means that the destination has a higher score than the origin for that lifestyle.

The vector X contains the mover's age group, sex, marital status, education and personal income, together with controls for race and ethnicity, citizenship and employment status. The coefficient vector β compares each group's OD lifestyle difference with that of its reference group. The term μ denotes origin-MSA fixed effects, τ denotes ACS-year fixed effects, and ε is the error term.

We estimate the six models using ACS person weights and cluster standard errors by origin MSA. The strict-match, complete-case sample contains 189,114 movers aged 18 or older, including a separate age group for those aged 65 and above.

The main model’s reference groups are age 18–24, male, married, less than high school, personal income below $25,000, non-Hispanic White, US citizen at birth and employed. Main 95% CIs use origin-MSA clustered standard errors.

ADDITIONAL ANALYSES

The full set of checks behind the paper.

The following sections reproduce the original supplementary analyses and all 13 supplementary figures. Open a section to read its design, findings and figures.

Two findings shape the interpretation.

Adding destination population and density reduces the travel contrasts for bachelor’s-or-higher and top-income movers from approximately 0.090 / 0.089 to 0.032 / 0.040. Separately, median split-half correlations of the area scores are only 0.11–0.40. These unresolved measurement and urban-context issues remain part of the study’s findings.

A2. Diary day of the week and the updated main resultsDiary weekday adjustment preserves the focal directions; it does not eliminate area-score measurement noise.

The ATUS oversamples weekend diary days. We therefore re-estimated all metropolitan lifestyle profiles with seven-category diary-day indicators, in addition to the original demographic and survey-year controls. The six activity totals, ten-year rolling windows, geographic matching rule, ACS sample, person weights, origin-MSA fixed effects and ACS-year fixed effects remain the same. All maps, linked origin–destination scores and the main regression figure were regenerated from these weekday-adjusted profiles.

A comparison with the archived pre-adjustment regression coefficients shows that the focal age, bachelor’s-degree and highest-income coefficient directions did not reverse. Across all 120 main-model coefficients, the median absolute coefficient change was 0.0013 standardized units; the largest was 0.0107 for the bachelor’s-degree coefficient in the work model. The updated main result remains N = 189,114 adult cross-MSA movers. These are specification comparisons rather than a claim that the weekday adjustment eliminates all uncertainty in local lifestyle measurement.

A3. Metropolitan examples, original minutes and coverageNamed metropolitan examples, adjusted minutes, population coverage and correlations among the six dimensions.

The top-five/bottom-five tables and maps identify concrete metropolitan examples for each of the six dimensions. For interpretability, we retain the adjusted ATUS area coefficients in minutes per diary day, alongside their standardized scores. The minutes shown in Supplementary Fig. 2 are each area’s adjusted coefficient minus the mean adjusted coefficient across the 172 areas used in the standardization; they are not the raw daily minutes of every resident. The 120 mapped MSAs account for 73.2% of the population across the 384 Census metropolitan areas in the 2022 population file. Their median 2022 population was 871,712, compared with 172,250 in the other 264 MSAs. The mapped sample is therefore concentrated in larger metropolitan areas.

Across the 120 mapped MSAs, the strongest pairwise correlations among the six adjusted scores are −0.41 for work versus leisure and −0.41 for social versus leisure. Work and travel correlate only 0.18, and household and leisure only 0.04. This does not support simply combining work and travel or treating the six scores as a single underlying scale.

Blue identifies ranks 1–5 and 6–10 at the high end; red identifies the corresponding low-end ranks. Rankings are separate for each dimension; other selected MSAs are grey.

Plotted minutes are adjusted ATUS area coefficients relative to the mean of the 172 areas used in standardization. The associated CSV lists metro names, counts, absolute coefficients and standardized scores.

A4. Expanded ACS characteristics and life-course interactionsFull demographics, household and work controls, plus age-by-education and age-by-income interactions.

The full baseline coefficient plot displays race/ethnicity, citizenship and employment, which were controlled for but omitted from Fig. 2. A separate robustness model adds children under age 18 in the household (ACS HUPAC), housing tenure (TEN), broad occupation bands (OCCP) and work-from-home travel mode (JWTR or JWTRNS). Household information was joined from the official ACS housing PUMS files for each survey year. The model retains the same 189,114 complete-case movers by assigning explicit “not applicable” groups where these variables do not apply. The education and income coefficients retain their principal directions in the expanded model: positive for work and travel, negative for household activity and leisure. These added characteristics are controls; their own coefficients should not be read as isolated effects of a change in family or work arrangement.

We also fit age-by-education and age-by-income interactions in separate models. The 15 age-by-education terms are jointly significant for personal care, household activity, social activity, leisure and travel, but not for work. The 15 age-by-income terms are jointly significant in all six outcomes. These joint tests show that age gradients vary with socioeconomic group, while individual cell contrasts should be interpreted cautiously. The age 18–24 and income US$100,000+ reference cell contains only 524 movers.

All model terms, including race/ethnicity, citizenship and employment; same strict sample and specification as main Fig. 2.

Age comparisons are shown within education groups; ACS person-weighted OLS with origin-MSA and year fixed effects.

Age comparisons are shown within income groups; interpret sparse young/high-income cells cautiously.

Grey is the main model; blue additionally adjusts for children in household, tenure, broad occupation and working from home. N = 189,114 in both.

A5. Geographic structure and alternative uncertainty estimatesDestination population and density attenuate travel contrasts; two-way clustering widens some intervals.

To assess whether the education and income results reflect urban form, we add destination-MSA log population and log gross population density to each main model. Population is from the Census Vintage 2022 metropolitan estimates, and area comes from the project’s CBSA boundary file. Both measures are fixed at 2022 and serve as broad cross-sectional controls rather than time-varying estimates of built-up density. The bachelor’s-degree and highest-income travel coefficients decrease from 0.090 and 0.089 to 0.032 and 0.040, respectively, but remain positive with 95% confidence intervals above zero. Work and leisure retain their main directions; the household coefficients weaken. Thus, metropolitan size and gross density explain part, but not all, of the travel contrast.

We additionally re-estimate standard errors clustered jointly by origin and destination MSA. Coefficient point estimates are unchanged, while some confidence intervals widen. The bachelor’s-degree contrasts for work, household activity, leisure and travel remain distinguishable from zero at the 95% level, as do the highest-income contrasts for household activity, leisure and travel. Several age contrasts, including the age-65-plus contrasts for social activity, leisure and travel, no longer exclude zero at 95%. The fixest package repaired four covariance matrices that were not positive definite; this is recorded as a numerical limitation of this alternative variance estimate.

Point estimates are unchanged; intervals use both origin- and destination-MSA clusters.

Grey is the main model; blue adds log 2022 destination-MSA population and log gross density. Main focus: education and income coefficients.

A6. Reliability of ATUS scores and sample thresholdsSplit-half area-score correlations remain low. Larger diary thresholds retain some directions but do not solve reliability.

For each of the ten rolling windows used in the ACS analysis (ending 2014–2023), we randomly split usable ATUS diaries into two non-overlapping halves with a fixed seed. We re-estimated the demographic-, year- and weekday-adjusted area scores independently in each half and correlated matched scores across the 120 selected MSAs. Median Pearson correlations across windows are 0.11 for work, 0.13 for household activity, 0.17 for leisure, 0.23 for personal care, 0.29 for travel and 0.40 for social activity. These low correlations indicate substantial noise in the local area scores at the current minimum of 100 diaries per ten-year window. Raising the score threshold to 200 or 300 diaries generally improves some correlations but leaves important uncertainty, especially for leisure.

As a sample-selection sensitivity check, we require both ends of an ACS move to have at least 200 or 300 ATUS diaries in the relevant ten-year window. The matched regression sample falls from 189,114 to 153,180 and 130,266 movers, respectively. The education and income travel coefficients remain positive in both restricted samples; the leisure contrasts remain negative. These checks do not remove the measurement-noise concern, and the score construction should be reviewed before submission.

Pearson correlation across 120 MSA scores estimated independently from two random halves, by rolling-window end year.

Origin and destination must each have at least 100, 200 or 300 ATUS respondents in the relevant ten-year window.

A7. Work-related travel versus other travelWork-related travel accounts for 17.3% of travel minutes; education and income contrasts are positive for both components.

Using the detailed ATUS activity code 180501, we separate travel related to working from all other Tier-1 travel activities and re-estimate each as its own standardized metropolitan score using the same demographic, survey-year and diary-day controls. Travel related to working accounts for 17.3% of all travel minutes recorded in the usable 2005–2025 diaries. In the strict ACS regression sample, both the bachelor’s-degree and highest-income coefficients are positive for work-related travel (0.116 and 0.095) and other travel (0.054 and 0.060). Because the two components are standardized separately, these coefficients cannot be added to reconstruct the original travel coefficient. This check indicates that the overall travel finding is not solely a commuting pattern.

Separate standardized outcomes using ATUS code 180501 for travel related to working. Same strict ACS movers and controls as main model.
